{{Short description|Concept in functional analysis}}
In mathematics, specifically in [[functional analysis]], a [[Family of sets|family]] <math>\mathcal{G}</math> of subsets a [[topological vector space]] (TVS) <math>X</math> is said to be '''saturated''' if <math>\mathcal{G}</math> contains a non-empty subset of <math>X</math> and if for every <math>G \in \mathcal{G},</math> the following conditions all hold:
# <math>\mathcal{G}</math> contains every subset of <math>G</math>; 
# the union of any finite collection of elements of <math>\mathcal{G}</math> is an element of <math>\mathcal{G}</math>; 
# for every scalar <math>a,</math> <math>\mathcal{G}</math> contains <math>aG</math>;
# the closed [[convex balanced hull]] of <math>G</math> belongs to <math>\mathcal{G}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=79–82}}

==Definitions==

If <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is any collection of subsets of <math>X</math> then the smallest saturated family containing <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is called the {{em|saturated hull}} of <math>\mathcal{S}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=79–82}} 

The family <math>\mathcal{G}</math> is said to {{em|cover}} <math>X</math> if the union <math>\bigcup_{G \in \mathcal{G}} G</math> is equal to <math>X</math>; 
it is {{em|total}} if the linear span of this set is a dense subset of <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=79–82}}

==Examples==

The intersection of an arbitrary family of saturated families is a saturated family.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=79–82}}
Since the [[power set]] of <math>X</math> is saturated, any given non-empty family <math>\mathcal{G}</math> of subsets of <math>X</math> containing at least one non-empty set, the saturated hull of <math>\mathcal{G}</math> is well-defined.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=79-88}} 
Note that a saturated family of subsets of <math>X</math> that covers <math>X</math> is a [[bornology]] on <math>X.</math>

The set of all [[Von Neumann bounded|bounded]] subsets of a [[topological vector space]] is a saturated family.
